questions.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\pm \text{i}.$*
${e}^{At}=\,\,$ $\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}} $\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$
questions.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -{\alpha }_{1}t \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\text{i}t) & ={e}^{\text{i}t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}\cdot \text{i}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{\alpha }_{1}t & =-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot t \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & =\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ 8 & -1\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $3,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
${e}^{At}={e}^{3t}\,\,$ $1+4t$ {{field-1}}
$8t$ {{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ 8 & -1\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 8{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(3t)={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t)={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
3t{e}^{3t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(1-3t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2{e}^{3t}t \\  & ={e}^{3t}(-2t) \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-{e}^{3t}t+{e}^{3t}(1-3t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(1-4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1+4t & -2t \\ 8t & 1-4t\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 \\ -8 & 2\end{aligned}].$ *Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $-2,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
${e}^{At}={e}^{-2t}\,\,$ $1-4t$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}} $1+4t$
questions.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 \\ -8 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t)={e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-2t)={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}(-2t){\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-2t{e}^{-2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}(1+2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(2t) \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & =-8{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(-8t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1-4t & 2t \\ -8t & 1+4t\end{aligned}].
$$
